english: I have a dog (I'm raising a dog)
usage: Polite; the everyday way to say you own/raise a pet
Progressive; stresses you currently have one
Swap 강아지 → 고양이 for a cat
examples: A: 혹시 반려동물 키워요? / B: 네, 강아지 키워요. 말티즈예요.
A: Do you have a pet? / B: Yes, I have a dog. It's a Maltese.
A/B exchange showing 키워요 as the natural response to a pet ownership question; breed names are used freely in Korean
집에서 고양이 두 마리 키워요.
I have two cats at home.
Count pets with 마리: 한 마리, 두 마리 — never 두 개
강아지 키운 지 3년 됐어요.
I've had my dog for 3 years.
-(으)ㄴ 지 ... 됐어요 = 'it's been ... since I started'; set phrase for elapsed time
nuance: 키우다 literally means 'to raise / bring up', and it is THE verb Koreans use for having a pet — you 'raise' a dog the same way you raise a child or grow a plant, so it carries warmth and active care. 강아지 키워요 is the polite-neutral form (존댓말), natural with anyone from a neighbor to a vet; with friends drop to 강아지 키워. The nearest near-synonym is 반려동물 있어요 ('I have a companion animal'), which is more formal/documentary and less the casual bonding opener 키워요 is. Variants: 키우고 있어요 (progressive, stressing ongoing care), 키워 본 적 있어요? (have you ever raised one?). The big English-speaker trap is translating 'I have a dog' as 강아지 있어요 — grammatically fine but means 'a dog is present here', not 'I own and care for one'; for pet ownership, 키워요 is mandatory. A second trap: 강아지 가지고 있어요 (using 가지다 'possess') treats the animal like an held object, which feels cold. Note 강아지 technically means 'puppy' but Koreans use it affectionately for any dog; the blunter neutral word 개 is used in compounds (개 짖는 소리) but sounds abrupt solo.

structuredNuance.t: 키우다 literally means 'to raise / bring up' — you raise a dog the same way you raise a child or grow a plant. 강아지 키워요 implies active, caring ownership; it is THE verb for having a pet, not just reporting that an animal exists nearby. 강아지 technically means 'puppy' but Koreans call any dog 강아지 affectionately; the neutral 개 sounds blunt used alone.

강아지 키워요 is polite-neutral 존댓말, comfortable with anyone — a neighbor, a vet, a new acquaintance. Drop to 강아지 키워 in 반말 with close friends. It's a natural small-talk opener that invites follow-up questions about breed and name.

강아지 있어요 means 'a dog is present (here)' — it reports existence, not caretaking ownership. 반려동물 있어요 is more formal and documentary. For the warm, relationship-based sense of 'I own and care for a pet', 키워요 is the only natural choice.
키우고 있어요 (progressive: 'I am currently raising'), 키운 지 N년 됐어요 ('it's been N years since I started'), 키워 본 적 있어요? ('have you ever raised one?'). Count animals with native numbers + 마리: 한 마리, 두 마리.

Trap 1: 강아지 있어요 for 'I have a dog' — this says the animal is present, not that you own it. Trap 2: 강아지 가지고 있어요 using 가지다 'possess' — treats a living animal like a held object, which sounds cold and strange. Always use 키우다 for pet ownership.

mistakes: Saying 강아지 있어요 to mean 'I have a dog'.
있어요 means 'exists / is here', so it reports a dog's presence, not that you own and care for one. For having a pet, say 강아지 키워요.
Saying 강아지 가지고 있어요.
가지다 ('to possess/hold') treats the animal like an object. A pet is 'raised', so use 키우다: 강아지 키워요.
Counting pets with 개 (the general counter).
Animals take the counter 마리: 강아지 두 마리. 개 is the counter for inanimate items (and also the word 'dog'), so 강아지 두 개 sounds wrong.

usage: 반말; what you say to your dog or a close friend
Polite, to a person (e.g. a partner)
Let's go (out) to take a walk
examples: A: 우리 강아지 산책 안 시키면 어떡해? / B: 알아, 지금 산책 가자!
A: What do we do if we don't walk the dog? / B: I know, let's go for a walk now!
A/B showing 산책 가자 as a casual, cheerful decision to head out; dogs learn the word 산책 fast
비 와서 오늘은 산책 못 가.
It's raining, so no walk today.
못 가 = 'can't go' (due to circumstance), softer than 안 가 ('won't go')
강아지 산책 좀 시키고 올게요.
I'll go walk the dog and be back.
산책시키다 = make the pet take a walk (causative); you make IT walk, you're not walking yourself
nuance: 산책 is 'a leisurely walk / stroll' (Sino-Korean 散策), and 산책 가다 = 'go for a walk' is the daily ritual every Korean dog owner knows. The crucial split English speakers miss is between 산책하다 / 산책 가다 (YOU go for a walk) and 산책시키다 (causative: you WALK THE DOG — make it take its walk). So you say 산책 가자 to your dog meaning 'let's both go', but report to others 강아지 산책시켜요 meaning 'I walk the dog (for it)'. Saying 강아지를 산책해요 is wrong — 산책하다 is intransitive and can't take a direct object; you need 산책시키다 to put the dog as object. To your dog, 반말 is totally normal; 산책 가자 or just 산책! is what owners shout. The nearest near-synonym invitation is 나가자 ('let's go out'), but 산책 가자 specifies the purpose is a walk. Note 산책 is for relaxed walking only — brisk exercise-walking is 걷기 운동, and a mountain hike is 등산, a completely different word; calling a mountain trip 산책 sounds odd. With a person (not your pet), use polite 산책 가요 unless you're close.

structuredNuance.t: 산책 (散策) means a leisurely stroll — not exercise-walking (걷기 운동) or hiking (등산). 산책 가자 means 'let's go take a stroll', an invitation that includes both speaker and listener. When said to a dog, it's a warm summons to go out together.
To your dog or a close friend: 반말 산책 가자. To a partner, coworker, or someone you've just met: polite 산책 가요. Koreans speak 반말 to pets routinely — 산책 가요 to a dog sounds unnaturally formal.

나가자 ('let's go out') is vaguer. 산책 가자 specifies the activity is a stroll. 산책시키다 vs 산책 가다: if you're walking the dog as its exercise routine (you're the agent making it walk), use the causative 산책시키다. If you're inviting it to come along, say 산책 가자.
산책하러 가자 (-하러 가다 = 'go to do'): stresses going OUT for the purpose. 산책 다녀올게요 ('I'll go for a walk and come back'): the return is implied. 산책 어때요? ('how about a walk?'): softened suggestion.
Trap 1: 강아지를 산책해요 for 'I walk the dog' — 산책하다 is intransitive; use the causative 산책시키다. Trap 2: calling a mountain hike 산책 — that is 등산. Trap 3: using 존댓말 산책 가요 to your own dog — pets get 반말.
산책 is 散策, a Sino-Korean word meaning leisurely walking/strolling.

mistakes: Saying 강아지를 산책해요 to mean 'I walk the dog'.
산책하다 is intransitive — only the walker can 'do' a walk. To walk a pet, use the causative 산책시키다: 강아지 산책시켜요.
Using 존댓말 to your own dog.
Koreans speak 반말 to pets. 산책 가요 to your dog sounds unnatural; say 산책 가자.
Calling a mountain hike 산책.
산책 is a gentle stroll. Hiking a mountain is 등산. 산에 산책 가요 sounds off — say 등산 가요.

english: What kind of food do you feed (your pet)?
usage: What food do you feed it?
Polite; asking another owner or a vet
Asking staff at a pet shop
examples: A: 강아지 사료 어떤 거 먹여요? / B: 저는 오리 고기 사료 먹이고 있어요.
A: What food do you feed your dog? / B: I'm feeding duck-meat kibble.
A/B exchange showing the full feed-question-and-answer pattern; 어떤 거 invites a category/brand answer
저희 고양이는 이 사료만 먹어요.
My cat only eats this food.
From the pet's side use 먹다 ('eats'), not 먹이다; the cat is subject here
수의사 선생님, 사료 어떤 거 먹이는 게 좋아요?
Doctor, what food is best to feed?
먹이는 게 좋아요 = 'it is good to feed (it)' — asking the vet for advice
nuance: 사료 is the specific word for animal feed or pet kibble (Sino-Korean 飼料) — do NOT call it 음식 or 밥 when referring to commercial pet food, though owners affectionately say 밥 먹자 ('let's eat') to the pet itself. The verb pair is the key trap: 먹다 = '(the pet) eats', while 먹이다 = '(I) feed / make eat' (causative). So 'I feed the dog kibble' is 강아지한테 사료를 먹여요, and 'the dog eats kibble' is 강아지가 사료를 먹어요. The nearest near-synonym question is 사료 뭐 먹여? (반말, same meaning), while 뭐 먹어요? ('what does it eat?') shifts to the pet's perspective with 먹다. The pet takes the recipient particle 한테 or formal 에게 — 강아지한테 먹여요; the phrasing 강아지를 먹여요 alone can sound like 'feeding ON the dog'. This phrase is polite-neutral, fitting for another owner, a 펫숍 clerk, or a vet. Note 어떤 거 ('which kind') invites a category/brand answer; 뭐 is more open. Don't confuse 사료 (staple kibble/feed) with 간식 ('treats/snacks') — asking about 사료 is about the daily diet.

structuredNuance.t: 사료 (飼料) is the specific term for commercial animal feed/kibble — not 음식 (human food) nor casual 밥. 사료 어떤 거 먹여요? literally asks 'what kind of feed do you feed it?' and is the standard way to inquire about another pet's diet.

사료 어떤 거 먹여요? is polite-neutral 존댓말, perfect with a stranger owner, a pet-shop clerk, or a vet. With a close friend: 사료 뭐 먹여? (반말). In a vet context you might say 사료 추천해 주세요 ('please recommend a food').

사료 어떤 거 먹여요? (what do you feed it?) vs. 사료 뭐 먹어요? (what does it eat?): the first focuses on the owner as feeder (먹이다 causative); the second focuses on the pet as eater (먹다). The former is more proactive ownership talk; the latter sounds like asking about the pet's preferences. Also: 사료 (daily diet) vs. 간식 (treats/snacks) — don't confuse them.
사료 바꿔 봤어요? ('have you tried switching food?'), 사료 추천해 주세요 ('please recommend a food'), 사료 성분 확인해 봤어요? ('have you checked the ingredients?').
사료 is 飼料, the Sino-Korean word for animal feed or fodder.

Trap 1: confusing 먹다 (pet eats) and 먹이다 (owner feeds) — use 먹이다 when YOU are the one providing the food. Trap 2: marking the pet with 를 as a direct object (강아지를 먹여요) without the food — it sounds like you're feeding ON the dog; add 한테: 강아지한테 사료를 먹여요. Trap 3: calling kibble 음식 — that is human food.

mistakes: Calling pet food 음식 or 밥 in a serious question.
Commercial pet food is 사료. 음식 is human food; use 사료 when asking a vet or shop: 사료 어떤 거 먹여요?
Saying 강아지가 사료 먹여요 to mean 'I feed the dog'.
먹이다 (feed) needs the feeder as subject and the pet as 한테: (제가) 강아지한테 사료를 먹여요. 강아지가 ... 먹여요 mixes up who eats and who feeds.
Marking the pet with 를 alone: 강아지를 먹여요.
The fed animal takes 한테/에게 for the recipient: 강아지한테 사료를 먹여요. 강아지를 먹여요 sounds like feeding on the dog.

english: I'll fill up your water bowl
usage: 반말, talking to your pet / casually
갈아 주다 = swap for fresh water
I should wash the food bowl
examples: A: 왜 이렇게 보채? / B: 아, 물그릇 비었네. 채워 줄게.
A: Why are you so fussy? / B: Oh, the water bowl is empty. I'll fill it.
A/B exchange showing 채워 줄게 as a caring response to a pet's behavior; 비다 = to be empty
고양이 물은 매일 갈아 줘야 돼요.
You should change a cat's water every day.
갈아 주다 = replace with fresh water, not just top up — hygiene distinction
밥 줬으니까 이제 물그릇만 채우면 돼.
I fed it, so now I just need to fill the water bowl.
...면 돼 = 'all I need to do is ...'; lists two care tasks
nuance: 물그릇 = 'water bowl' (물 'water' + 그릇 'bowl'), and 밥그릇 = 'food bowl' — Koreans use these compound words naturally for pet dishes. The verb choices carry real distinctions: 채우다 = 'to fill up' (add water to an existing amount), 갈다 = 'to change / replace' (dump and refill with fresh), 비우다 = 'to empty'. In daily pet care, 갈아 주다 is the hygiene-conscious verb because cats especially need fresh water; just 채우다 implies you topped up old water. The -아/어 줄게 form ('I'll do it for you / as a favor') and -아/어 줄게 / -아/어 줘 ('do it for me') express care-giving, which is the natural register owners use toward pets in 반말. The nearest near-synonym action would be 물 넣어 줘 ('put water in'), which is understandable but less idiomatically pet-specific than 채우다/갈아 주다. Don't confuse 그릇 ('bowl, round vessel') with 접시 ('flat plate') — pets use 그릇, not 접시. Speaking to a person helping you: 물 좀 채워 주세요 (polite). The -줄게 ending is self-directed ('I'll do it'), so you say it to your pet; 갈아 줘 or 채워 줘 is what you ask of a family member helping.

structuredNuance.t: 물그릇 채워 줄게 literally means 'I'll fill up the water bowl for you' — 채우다 = to fill, 줄게 = I'll do it (as a favor/for you). It's directed at the pet in 반말 and expresses the caring daily routine of checking and refilling water.

반말 with the affectionate -줄게 (-아/어 줄게) is the natural register when talking to your pet. To a family member helping: 물 좀 채워 줘 (반말) or 물 좀 채워 주세요 (polite). 줄게 is self-directed; 줘/주세요 is a request to someone else.

채우다 vs. 갈아 주다: 채우다 = add more water (top up), 갈아 주다 = dump the old and replace with fresh. For daily care, 갈아 주다 is the hygiene-minded choice. 물 넣어 줘 ('put water in') works but is more generic. Never 접시 for a pet bowl — use 그릇.
물 갈아 줄게 ('I'll change your water'), 밥그릇 씻어야겠다 ('I'd better wash the food bowl'), 물 다 마셨네 ('it drank all the water, huh').

Trap 1: reaching for generic 만들다 or 넣다 — the idiomatic care-verbs are 채우다 and 갈아 주다. Trap 2: using 접시 (a flat plate) for a pet bowl — pets use 그릇: 물그릇, 밥그릇. Trap 3: over-formal 채워 드릴게요 toward a pet — 드리다 honors people, not animals; keep it 반말 with -줄게.

mistakes: Saying 물 채워 줘 when you mean 'give fresh water'.
채우다 just adds water to what's there. To replace stale water with clean, say 물 갈아 줘 ('change the water').
Using 접시 for the water dish.
접시 is a flat plate. A pet's bowl is 그릇: 물그릇, 밥그릇.
Over-formal 채워 드릴게요 toward your pet.
Honorifics like 드리다 are for elevating people. To a pet, 반말 is normal: 물그릇 채워 줄게.

english: I have to pick up the poop
usage: I have to pick up the poop
Polite-neutral; 응가 = cute word for poop
반말; 똥 is blunter than 응가
Did you grab a poop bag?
오줌 (을) 싸다 = to pee; 쌌어 = peed
examples: A: 여기서 잠깐만요. / B: 왜요? / A: 강아지 응가 치워야 돼요.
A: One moment here. / B: What? / A: I have to pick up the poop.
A/B exchange showing the phrase arising naturally during a walk
배변봉투로 똥 치우고 왔어.
I picked up the poop with a bag and came back.
배변봉투로 = 'using a waste bag' (instrument 로); 똥 is more blunt than 응가 but fine among friends
우리 강아지 아직 화장실 못 가려요.
My dog isn't potty-trained yet.
화장실 가리다 = to be house-trained / able to control toileting; lit. 'distinguish the bathroom'
nuance: 치우다 = 'to clear away / clean up / pick up', the precise verb for scooping pet waste — not 청소하다 ('clean a room/surface'), which is too broad for a single pick-up action. For the waste itself, register matters: 응가 is soft and slightly babyish ('poop / number two'), widely used by owners and parents, and appropriate in polite company; 똥 is the plain, blunter everyday word for 'poop/crap', fine in 반말; and 대변 is the clinical/formal term used with a vet. A 배변봉투 ('defecation bag') is what you must carry on walks — scooping is both social etiquette and, in many Korean municipalities, the law. The nearest near-synonym command is 똥 치워 (반말, same action), so the register difference between 응가/똥/대변 is the main dividing line. Potty-training is 화장실(을) 가리다 (lit. 'to distinguish the bathroom'), and peeing is 오줌(을) 싸다 or politely 소변 보다. The English-speaker trap is 응가 잡다 — 잡다 = 'grab/catch a moving thing', completely wrong; you 치우다 ('clear away') waste. Don't say 응가 만들다 either.

structuredNuance.t: 응가 치워야 돼요 means 'I have to clear away the poop' — 치우다 = clear/pick up (not clean a surface), 돼요 = it's required/I have to. The phrase is casual but polite, naturally said to a companion during a dog walk.

응가 is the soft polite register; use it around strangers or in mixed company. 똥 works in 반말 among friends. In a vet's office use 대변/소변. Scooping is legally required in most Korean cities during public walks.

응가 (soft/cute) vs. 똥 (blunt/casual) vs. 대변 (clinical). 치우다 vs. 청소하다: 청소 is for cleaning an area; 치우다 is for removing a discrete item of waste. 화장실 가리다 = potty-trained; 오줌 싸다 = pee (don't confuse with 소변 보다, the polite form).
응가 치웠어요 ('I picked it up', reported), 배변봉투 꼭 챙기세요 ('be sure to bring a poop bag'), 아직 응가 못 가려요 ('it can't control bowels yet', about an untrained puppy).
Trap 1: 응가 잡다 — 잡다 = grab something moving; waste is 치우다. Trap 2: 청소하다 for scooping one poop — 청소 is area-cleaning. Trap 3: using 똥 with a vet — clinical contexts require 대변/소변.

mistakes: Saying 응가 잡다 to mean 'pick up the poop'.
잡다 = grab/catch (something moving). For cleaning up waste use 치우다: 응가 치워야 돼요.
Using 청소하다 for scooping a single poop.
청소하다 = clean (a whole area). For picking up pet waste, the verb is 치우다.
Saying 똥 in a formal vet conversation.
똥 is blunt/casual. In a clinic, use 대변 (feces) and 소변 (urine): 대변 색이 이상해요.

english: Does it need to get vaccinated?
usage: I got it the rabies shot
주사 맞히다 = have (it) get a shot
examples: A: 선생님, 이번에 어떤 예방접종 맞아야 돼요? / B: 종합백신이랑 광견병 맞으세요.
A: Doctor, what vaccinations does it need this time? / B: Give it the combo vaccine and rabies shot.
A/B vet exchange using 맞다 (pet receives shot); 종합백신 = combination/multi-vaccine
이번에 광견병 예방접종 맞혔어요.
I had it get the rabies vaccine this time.
맞히다 (causative) = I had/made it receive the shot; owner is the agent
접종 기록 카드 가지고 오세요.
Bring the vaccination record card.
접종 기록 = vaccination record (the clinic gives you a card to keep)
nuance: 예방접종 = 'preventive vaccination' (예방 prevention + 접종 'inoculation'), the umbrella word for pet shots; 광견병 = rabies, a key annual vaccine. The verb structure is a classic learner minefield: 주사/접종을 맞다 = '(the patient) receives a shot' — in Korean the receiver 'gets hit' by the shot; 맞히다 is the causative = '(I) have it receive a shot'. So your dog 주사를 맞아요 ('gets the shot'), and you 주사를 맞혔어요 ('had it vaccinated'). The nearest near-synonym phrase is 주사 맞았어요 ('got the shot'), which swaps 예방접종 for 주사 but uses the same verb. English speakers wrongly import 'inject' as 주사하다 about themselves — for receiving, it's 맞다; saying 주사를 해요 or 주사를 때려요 are both wrong. This phrase is polite-neutral, perfect for the 동물병원. Note: 동물병원 ('animal hospital') is the standard word for a vet clinic — the vet is 수의사(선생님). Keep your 접종 기록 (vaccine record) safe; clinics ask for it.

structuredNuance.t: 예방접종 (예방+접종, prevention+inoculation) literally means preventive vaccination. 맞아야 돼요? = 'does it need to receive (it)?', using 맞다 = to receive a shot, literally 'to be hit'. The question politely asks the vet about the pet's vaccination schedule.
Polite-neutral 존댓말, exactly right for the vet. In casual chat with another owner: 예방접종 했어? (반말). The vet is 수의사(선생님); the clinic is 동물병원 — never just 병원 (human hospital).
예방접종 맞아야 돼요? vs. 주사 맞아야 돼요?: 예방접종 specifies a scheduled preventive vaccine; 주사 is any injection. 맞다 (pet receives it) vs. 맞히다 (owner causes it): 강아지가 주사를 맞아요 vs. (내가) 강아지한테 주사를 맞혔어요.
접종 기록 확인해 주세요 ('please check the vaccine record'), 추가 접종 필요해요? ('does it need a booster?'), 예방접종 스케줄 알려 주세요 ('please tell me the vaccination schedule').

Trap 1: 주사를 해요 or 주사하다 for getting a shot — for receiving, it's 맞다: 주사를 맞아요. Trap 2: confusing 맞다 (pet gets it) with 맞히다 (you make it get it) — pick by who's doing what. Trap 3: 병원 alone for the vet clinic — say 동물병원.

mistakes: Saying 주사를 해요 / 주사하다 for getting a shot.
To receive an injection, Korean uses 맞다: 주사를 맞아요. 주사하다 isn't how you say 'get a shot'.
Confusing 맞다 (the pet gets it) with 맞히다 (you have it get it).
강아지가 주사를 맞아요 = the dog gets the shot. (제가) 강아지한테 주사를 맞혔어요 = I had it vaccinated. Pick by who's doing what.
Calling the vet clinic 병원 only.
병원 alone implies a human hospital. The vet is 동물병원: 동물병원 가야 돼요.

usage: I'd like to book the clinic
Saying it to the clinic / on the phone
진료 받다 = receive a medical exam
examples: A: 오늘 강아지 좀 이상해 보여요. / B: 동물병원 예약했어요? / A: 네, 오늘 오후 예약했어요.
A: The dog looks a bit off today. / B: Did you make a vet appointment? / A: Yes, I booked this afternoon.
A/B exchange showing 예약하다 as the natural step after noticing a health concern
강아지 진료 예약하려고 전화했어요.
I called to book my dog's exam.
진료 = medical consultation/exam; distinguishes from mere 예약 (booking)
접수처에서 이름이랑 증상 말씀하세요.
Tell them the name and symptoms at reception.
접수처 = the reception desk; 증상 = symptoms — give these on arrival, not just 예약
nuance: 예약하다 = 'to reserve / book' (an appointment, table, ticket), and 동물병원 예약 is how you book a vet visit. Korean clinics have three distinct steps English speakers often collapse: 예약 (book in advance), 접수 (check in / register on arrival at the desk), and 진료 (the actual exam/consultation from the doctor). You 예약하다 by phone or app, 접수하다 at the desk on arrival, then 진료(를) 받다 ('receive an exam'). The nearest near-synonym is 진료 예약했어요, which is slightly more specific. A critical error: 약속 means 'a promise / personal plans with someone', not a booked business appointment — say 예약, not 약속. Also, 진료 받다 uses 받다 ('to receive') — YOU receive the exam from the doctor; saying 진료해요 about yourself is wrong (진료하다 is what the doctor does). The clinic will call you 보호자분 ('guardian'), which is how Korean vets refer to pet owners — a telling sign of how seriously pet ownership is treated. This phrase is polite-neutral.

structuredNuance.t: 예약하다 = 'to reserve / book' — 동물병원 예약했어요 reports that you've booked a vet visit in advance. It is the standard phrase whether you booked by phone, app, or in person.
Polite-neutral 존댓말, correct for reporting to family, another owner, or the clinic itself. On the phone to book: 강아지 진료 예약하고 싶은데요 ('I'd like to book my dog for an exam'). At arrival: 접수 먼저 할게요.

예약 (book in advance) vs. 접수 (check in on arrival) vs. 진료 (the actual exam): these are three separate steps — using only 예약 for all three confuses the staff. 약속 is a personal promise/plan with a person, not a booked service appointment — never 동물병원 약속했어요.
예약 취소할게요 ('I'll cancel the appointment'), 예약 변경하고 싶어요 ('I'd like to change the appointment'), 당일 예약 돼요? ('do you accept same-day bookings?').

Trap 1: 약속 for a vet appointment — 약속 is for personal social plans; booked services are 예약. Trap 2: 진료해요 about yourself — 진료하다 is the doctor's action; the patient side is 진료(를) 받다. Trap 3: skipping 접수 when you arrive — Koreans always check in (접수) at the desk first.

mistakes: Using 약속 for a clinic appointment.
약속 is a promise / plans with a person. A booked business appointment is 예약: 동물병원 예약했어요.
Saying 진료해요 to mean 'I'm getting an exam'.
진료하다 is what the doctor does (examines). The patient side is 진료(를) 받다: 진료 받으러 왔어요.
Skipping 접수 and going straight to the vet.
Korean clinics have you 접수 (check in) at the desk first. Say 접수 먼저 할게요 on arrival, then wait to be called.

english: Where does it hurt? / What's wrong?
usage: What the vet asks; you describe the symptom
안 먹어요 = refuses food (a key symptom)
토하다 = to throw up; 계속 = continuously
examples: A: 어디가 아파요? / B: 어제부터 밥을 안 먹고 자꾸 토해요.
A: What's wrong / where does it hurt? / B: Since yesterday it won't eat and keeps throwing up.
A/B vet exchange showing the expected answer format: onset (어제부터) + specific symptoms
고양이가 자꾸 토하고 기운이 없어요.
The cat keeps throwing up and has no energy.
기운이 없다 = to be lethargic / low energy — key symptom to name; 자꾸 = repeatedly
여기를 만지면 아파하는 것 같아요.
It seems to hurt when I touch here.
아파하다 = to show/express pain (for observed others); -것 같다 = 'it seems'; use 아파하다, not 아프다, for the pet
nuance: 아프다 = 'to be sick / hurt / in pain', and 어디가 아파요? ('where does it hurt?') is the vet's opening question — you'll mainly ANSWER by describing symptoms concretely. A subtle but important grammatical point: 아프다 describes YOUR OWN felt pain, but for an animal or another person whose pain you are observing from outside, Korean uses 아파하다 ('to show/exhibit pain') — so 강아지가 아파해요 ('the dog is showing signs of pain') is the careful form; casually owners say 아파요 too and it's understood. The nearest near-synonym question is 뭐가 문제예요? ('what's the problem?'), which is more general; 어디가 아파요? specifically invites a body-area or symptom answer. Key symptom vocabulary: 토하다 (vomit — NOT 뱉다 which is deliberate spitting), 설사하다 (have diarrhea), 절다 (limp), 기운이 없다 (lethargic), 안 먹다 (won't eat). English speakers often say 'sick' and stop — but Korean vets expect the onset (언제부터, 'since when') and the concrete symptom. Give time with -부터: 어제부터, 아침부터.

structuredNuance.t: 어디가 아파요? literally asks 'where is it that it hurts?' — a vet's diagnostic opener. When you hear this question, the expected answer is the onset time (언제부터) + the specific symptom(s), not just 'sick'.
Polite-neutral 존댓말, used by the vet asking you. Your answer should also be polite (존댓말) since you're talking to a professional. Use clinical terms in a vet context: 대변/소변, 구토, 설사, 식욕부진.

아프다 (I feel pain — self-referential) vs. 아파하다 (observed other shows pain). A dog 아파해요, not 아프다, when you're describing what you see. Also: 토하다 (vomit) vs. 뱉다 (deliberately spit out) — dogs 토해요, they don't 뱉어요.
증상이 어떻게 돼요? ('what are the symptoms?'), 언제부터 그랬어요? ('since when has it been like this?'), 아파하는 부위가 있어요? ('is there a specific area where it shows pain?').

Trap 1: saying only '아파요' without a symptom or onset — vets need 언제부터 + what symptom. Trap 2: 아프다 for an animal (strictly for self-reported pain): use 아파하다 for observed pain. Trap 3: 뱉어요 for vomiting — 뱉다 = spit deliberately; vomiting is 토하다.

mistakes: Saying only '아파요' without naming the symptom.
Vets need specifics. Add the symptom and onset: 어제부터 밥을 안 먹고 토해요.
Using 아프다 vs. 아파하다 loosely for the pet.
Strictly, you feel 아프다; an animal you observe 아파하다 (shows pain). 강아지가 아파해요 is the careful form.
Saying 뱉어요 to mean 'it vomits'.
뱉다 = spit out (deliberately). Vomiting is 토하다: 자꾸 토해요.

examples: A: 중성화 수술 했어요? / B: 네, 작년에 수술했어요. 지금은 완전히 회복됐어요.
A: Is it neutered/spayed? / B: Yes, it had surgery last year. It's fully recovered now.
A/B exchange showing 중성화 했어요? as a standard owner-to-owner question
중성화 하면 성격이 좀 차분해져요.
Neutering makes them a bit calmer.
차분해지다 = to become calm/settled; owners discuss behavioral benefits
수술한 데 핥지 못하게 넥카라 씌웠어요.
I put a cone on so it can't lick the incision.
넥카라 (neck collar/Elizabethan cone) = the protective cone; 씌우다 = put it on (over the head)
nuance: 중성화 = 'neutering / spaying' (中性化, lit. 'making neutral in sex'), and critically this one word covers BOTH male neutering AND female spaying — unlike English, Korean doesn't need separate terms. 중성화 수술 했어요 is the standard polite phrase between owners and at the vet. The verb 수술(을) 하다 = 'to have/do surgery'; from the owner's side 했어요 is natural even though technically the vet performs it — Korean lets the responsible party say 했어요. The nearest near-synonym is 거세 했어요 ('castrated'), but 거세 is blunt and clinical, used only for male animals in clinical or agricultural settings; for a pet, 중성화 is always more appropriate. Saying 고쳤어요 ('I fixed it', using 고치다 = repair a broken thing) is a direct English-trap error — the procedure is not 'fixing' an object. Related care vocabulary: 넥카라 (the protective Elizabethan cone, from 'neck collar'), 회복 ('recovery'), 수술 부위 ('surgical site'), 핥다 ('to lick' — pets must be prevented from licking the wound). Keep 수술 with 하다/받다.

structuredNuance.t: 중성화 (中性化) literally means 'making neutral/neuter in sex' — it applies to both males and females, covering both English concepts 'neuter' and 'spay' with a single word. 중성화 수술 했어요 reports the procedure is done.

Polite-neutral 존댓말, standard between owners and at the vet. 중성화 했어요? is a very common get-to-know-your-pet question among dog park acquaintances — it's not considered rude. With a close friend: 중성화 했어? (반말).

중성화 covers both sexes — no need for separate 'neuter' vs. 'spay' distinctions. 거세 (castration) is the literal clinical/agricultural term for males; it feels blunt or harsh for a pet. 고치다 ('repair/fix') is wrong entirely — it's for broken objects, not living beings.
중성화 수술 받았어요 ('it received the surgery' — pet-side perspective), 회복 중이에요 ('in recovery'), 수술 부위 잘 낫고 있어요 ('the surgical site is healing well').
중성화 is 中性化, 'making neuter/neutral in sex'. The -화 (化) suffix means 'making X' or 'becoming X', as in 현대화 (modernization), 자동화 (automation).

Trap 1: 거세 — too blunt/clinical for pet talk; use 중성화. Trap 2: 고쳤어요 for 'got it fixed' — 고치다 = repair an object; the procedure is 중성화 수술 했어요. Trap 3: thinking 중성화 only means male neutering — it covers females (spaying) equally.

mistakes: Using 거세 for a pet's neutering.
거세 (castration) is blunt/clinical. The standard, gentle term for both sexes is 중성화: 중성화 수술 했어요.
Saying 고쳤어요 to mean 'got it fixed/neutered'.
고치다 = repair a broken thing. For the procedure say 중성화 수술 했어요, not 고쳤어요.
Assuming 중성화 only means male neutering.
중성화 covers spaying females too. You don't switch words by sex — 암컷도 중성화 한다 ('females are also neutered').

usage: Polite; ask BEFORE petting a stranger's dog
examples: A: 강아지 만져도 돼요? / B: 네, 안 물어요. 순해요.
A: May I pet your dog? / B: Yes, it doesn't bite. It's gentle.
A/B exchange modeling the essential stranger-dog etiquette sequence
저희 강아지는 안 물어요, 순해요.
My dog doesn't bite, it's gentle.
순하다 = good-natured, docile; reassures the asker fully
낯선 사람 보면 좀 짖어요, 물진 않아요.
It barks a bit at strangers, but it doesn't bite.
짖다 = to bark; distinguishes barking from biting — an important nuance for nervous strangers
nuance: 물다 = 'to bite', and 물어요? plus 만져도 돼요? ('may I pet it?') are the two essential phrases to say before touching a stranger's dog — social etiquette in Korea. The permission frame -아도 돼요? = 'is it okay if I...?' applies here for approach. The nearest near-synonym pair for the answer side is 순해요 (gentle/docile) vs. 사나워요 (fierce/aggressive) — knowing these lets you reassure OR warn. The critical sound-alike trap: 물다 (bite) sounds similar to 묻다 (ask / bury / stain) — both give 물어요 in present tense; only context (a dog) tells you apart. Also confuse learners: 짖다 = 'to bark' (noise, not necessarily dangerous), 으르렁거리다 = 'to growl' (warning sign), 물다 = 'to bite' (action) — a barking dog isn't necessarily a biting one. Don't say 물기 해요 or import 'bite' oddly; the plain present tense of 물다 is 물어요. Petting culture: always ask 만져도 돼요? first — reaching out silently can startle the dog and annoy its owner, even if the dog is friendly. This is polite-neutral.

structuredNuance.t: 물어요? literally means 'does it bite?' — from 물다 'to bite', conjugated politely. It is the essential safety question before touching any dog you don't know. Paired naturally with 만져도 돼요? as a two-part permission-and-safety check.

Polite-neutral 존댓말, perfect for approaching a stranger with a dog. With friends asking about your dog informally: 물어? (반말). Petting culture: always ask before reaching out — silent approach is impolite and can startle the animal.

물다 (bite) vs. 짖다 (bark) vs. 으르렁거리다 (growl): these are three distinct behaviors. A barking dog (짖어요) is not necessarily biting. The temperament vocabulary: 순하다 (gentle/docile) vs. 사납다 (fierce/aggressive) vs. 낯을 가리다 (shy around strangers).
물 것 같아요 ('it looks like it might bite', caution), 잘 안 물어요 ('it rarely bites'), 처음에는 짖는데 금방 친해져요 ('it barks at first but warms up quickly').

Trap 1: confusing 물다 (bite) and 묻다 (ask/bury) — both give 물어요; a dog 물어요? = 'does it bite?', not 'does it ask?'. Trap 2: saying 물기 해요 — the plain verb 물다 conjugates 물어요 without any extra structure. Trap 3: confusing 짖다 (bark) with 물다 (bite) in descriptions.

mistakes: Confusing 물다 (bite) with 짖다 (bark).
물어요? = does it bite? 짖어요 = it barks. A barking dog isn't necessarily biting — use the right verb.
Petting a stranger's dog without asking.
Always ask first: 만져도 돼요? 물어요? Reaching out silently can startle the dog and annoy the owner.
Mixing 물다 (bite) and 묻다 (ask).
Both can surface as 물어요, but from different verbs. With a dog, 물어요? = 'does it bite?' Keep the base verbs straight.

english: Please put it on a leash
examples: A: 여기는 목줄 꼭 해 주세요. / B: 아, 죄송해요. 지금 할게요.
A: Please keep it on a leash here. / B: Oh, sorry. I'll do it now.
A/B exchange of a gentle reminder about the leash rule — 꼭 = without fail
대형견은 입마개도 해야 돼요.
Large dogs must also wear a muzzle.
대형견 = large-breed dog; 입마개 = muzzle; legally required in Korea for certain breeds
엘리베이터에서는 안아 주시거나 목줄 짧게요.
In the elevator, hold it or keep the leash short.
안다 = to hold in arms; 짧게(요) = keep it short — elevator etiquette in apartment buildings
nuance: 목줄 = 'leash / collar-lead' (목 'neck' + 줄 'cord/line'), the standard everyday word; 가슴줄 / 하네스 = 'harness' (chest lead, for dogs prone to neck strain). 목줄 (을) 하다 or 채우다 = 'to put on / fasten a leash'. In Korea, leashing your dog in public is legally required, and certain large or aggressive breeds must also wear an 입마개 ('muzzle', 입 'mouth' + 마개 'plug/stopper'). The nearest near-synonym action is 목줄 채워 주세요 (slightly more specific: 'please fasten the leash on'), while 묶어 주세요 (tie it up) would imply tethering to a fixed object — a distinct concept. The English-speaker trap is calling a leash 끈 (generic 'string/strap') — understandable but 목줄 is the specific proper term. Don't use 묶다 for routine walking; 묶다 implies tying to a post and doesn't match leash-walking. The verb 채우다 here means 'to fasten/clip' — same verb as filling a bowl, but context tells you apart: leash = fasten, bowl = fill. This phrase is polite, exactly right for asking another owner or leaving a note in a community. Korean apartment etiquette: in elevators, many owners 안아요 (carry) small dogs or keep the 목줄 짧게 (short) as a courtesy.

structuredNuance.t: 목줄 (목=neck + 줄=cord) = leash/collar-lead. 해 주세요 = please do (it) for (me/us), a polite request. 목줄 해 주세요 is both a courteous reminder and, in public spaces, a reference to a legal requirement. 입마개 (입=mouth + 마개=plug) = muzzle.
목줄 해 주세요 is polite 존댓말, ideal for asking a stranger owner. In apartment communities or parks, a sign might say 반드시 목줄 착용 ('leash required without exception'). With a family member: 목줄 해 줘 (반말).

목줄 하다 / 채우다 (fasten the leash, for walking) vs. 묶다 (tie to a fixed point, like a post). Use 목줄 채우다 for leashing during a walk; 묶어 두다 for tying the dog to something. 끈 (generic string) is too vague — use 목줄 specifically.
목줄 착용 의무 ('mandatory leash requirement', official signage), 목줄 채웠어요? ('did you put the leash on?', checking), 하네스로 바꿨어요 ('I switched to a harness').

Trap 1: 끈 for a leash — too generic; use 목줄 (or 하네스/가슴줄 for a harness). Trap 2: 묶어 주세요 for 'please leash it' — 묶다 = tie to a post, not leash-walk; say 목줄 해 주세요. Trap 3: forgetting 입마개 — some large breeds legally need a muzzle, not just a leash.

mistakes: Calling a leash just 끈.
끈 is a generic strap/string. The specific word is 목줄 (leash) or 하네스/가슴줄 (harness).
Using 묶다 for leashing on a walk.
묶다 = tie up (to a post). Routine leashing is 목줄 하다 / 잡다. Say 목줄 해 주세요, not 묶어 주세요, for normal walks.
Forgetting the muzzle term 입마개.
Some large breeds legally need a muzzle: 입마개. Don't invent 입 가리개; the standard word is 입마개.

english: It was so cute that I adopted it
usage: Polite; 입양 = adoption (of a pet or child)
I brought it from a shelter
examples: A: 어디서 데려왔어요? / B: 유기견 보호소에서 입양했어요. 처음에는 좀 무서워했어요.
A: Where did you get it from? / B: I adopted it from a shelter. At first it was a bit scared.
A/B exchange showing 입양하다 in context of a shelter rescue; 무서워하다 = to be scared
유기견 보호소에서 강아지 데려왔어요.
I brought a dog home from a shelter.
데려오다 = bring home a living being — warmer and correct; 가져오다 = bring an object (wrong for animals)
펫숍에서 분양받는 것보다 입양이 좋아요.
Adopting beats buying from a pet shop.
분양받다 (acquire from a breeder/shop) contrasted with 입양하다 (adopt a rescue)
nuance: 입양 = 'adoption' (入養), used for both adopting a child and taking in a pet — 입양했어요 is the warm, socially valued word for giving a rescue animal a home. The key contrast is 입양 (adopt from a shelter/rescue) vs. 분양 (acquire from a breeder or pet shop, usually for a fee). Animal-welfare-minded Koreans cite the slogan 사지 말고 입양하세요 ('don't buy, adopt'). The verb for bringing the animal home is 데려오다 ('to bring a person/animal along') — the verb 데리다 marks the animal as a companion being, not a thing; using 가져오다 ('bring an object') for a pet sounds cold and wrong. The nearest near-synonym phrase is 보호소에서 데려왔어요, which focuses on the action of bringing it home; 입양했어요 formally names the relationship (adoption). The English-speaker trap is using 사다 ('to buy') — while pets can be purchased, 사다 in casual pet conversation sounds blunt or mercenary; 분양받다 or 입양하다 are the natural choices. Another trap: 채택하다 = 'adopt (a plan/idea)' — completely wrong for a living being. This is polite-neutral; related terms: 보호소 (shelter), 임시보호 ('temporary fostering'), 유기 ('abandonment / being abandoned').

structuredNuance.t: 입양 (入養) literally means 'entering and raising' — it is the formal but commonly used word for adopting a child or a pet from a rescue situation. 예뻐서 입양했어요 = 'I adopted it because it was so cute', explaining the personal motivation behind adoption.

Polite-neutral 존댓말. 입양하다 is used in both formal and casual speech. Animal welfare culture in Korea increasingly values 입양 over purchasing; saying 입양했어요 often prompts warm responses from fellow owners.

입양하다 (adopt from shelter/rescue, usually free or donation) vs. 분양받다 (acquire from breeder/shop, usually paid). Also: 데려오다 (bring a living being home — correct for pets) vs. 가져오다 (bring an object — wrong for animals). 채택하다 = adopt a plan/idea, not a living being.
입양 is 入養, literally 'entering and raising/nurturing', used for both child adoption and pet adoption in Korean.

Trap 1: 사다 ('buy') for getting a pet — sounds blunt/mercenary; use 분양받다 (paid acquisition) or 입양하다 (rescue/adoption). Trap 2: 채택하다 — that's adopting a plan or proposal, not a living being. Trap 3: 가져왔어요 for bringing the pet home — use 데려왔어요 (came with a living being).

mistakes: Saying 가져왔어요 about bringing a pet home.
가져오다 is for objects. For a living animal use 데려오다: 보호소에서 데려왔어요.
Using 채택하다 for adopting an animal.
채택하다 = adopt a plan/idea. Adopting a pet (or child) is 입양하다: 강아지를 입양했어요.
Calling shelter adoption 분양.
분양 implies obtaining (often buying) from a breeder/shop. Taking in a rescue is 입양; the source is a 보호소.

usage: Asking a pet's age; answer in 살
Is it a boy or a girl?
examples: A: 강아지 이름이 뭐예요? / B: 콩이예요. 우리 애기예요, 완전 가족이에요.
A: What's your dog's name? / B: It's Kong-i. It's our baby — totally part of the family.
A/B exchange showing how pet owners naturally frame their pet as family; -이 suffix on pet names ending in a consonant (콩 → 콩이)
우리 집 막내, 세 살이에요.
Our youngest, three years old.
막내 = youngest family member; pets are placed in the family birth-order naturally
남자아이예요, 이름은 콩이예요.
It's a boy, his name's Kong-i.
남자아이 = boy (for pets); -이 suffix on 콩 is endearing
nuance: Korean pet owners overwhelmingly treat pets as family, so 우리 애기예요 ('this is our baby') is genuine daily speech, not embarrassing baby-talk. The word 우리 ('our/my') is crucial: Koreans instinctively say 우리 강아지, 우리 고양이 rather than 제 강아지, treating the pet as shared family — 제 (my, formal possessive) for a beloved pet sounds oddly distancing. The nearest near-synonym phrase is 우리 가족이에요 ('it's our family member'), which is equally natural. Owners refer to a pet's sex as 남자아이 / 여자아이 ('boy / girl') rather than blunt 수컷 ('male') / 암컷 ('female'), which sound clinical/livestock-like in casual conversation. Ages use native numbers + 살: 세 살 (3 years old), 다섯 살 (5 years old). The endearing -이 suffix attaches to pet names ending in a consonant (콩 → 콩이, 별 → 별이), making them sound warmer. The English-speaker trap is the formal dictionary phrase 제 애완동물 — 애완동물 is correct but stiff and slightly dated; the warm modern term is 반려동물 ('companion animal'), and in affectionate speech people just say 우리 애기/강아지. This register is casual-affectionate but maintains 존댓말 endings (예요) with strangers.

structuredNuance.t: 우리 애기예요 literally means 'it is our baby' — 애기 is an affectionate form of 아기 ('baby'). This is not ironic or embarrassing; it reflects the genuine family-member status pets hold in Korean household culture. The -이에요 ending is warm polite speech.

Casual-affectionate but socially appropriate; 존댓말 endings (예요) with strangers. Among close friends or talking to the pet itself: 우리 애기야 (반말). This framing is expected and normal in Korean pet culture — you won't sound strange saying it.

우리 vs. 제: always 우리 강아지 (ours, family sense), not 제 강아지 (my own, formal-possessive), for beloved pets — 제 sounds distancing. 남자아이/여자아이 (casual sex reference) vs. 수컷/암컷 (clinical/breeding terms). 반려동물 (warm modern term) vs. 애완동물 (older, slightly dated).
우리 가족이에요 ('it's our family'), 우리 막내예요 ('our youngest'), 이름은 ...이에요/예요 ('its name is ...'). Pet name suffix: consonant-ending name + -이 (콩이, 별이, 밥이); vowel-ending name as-is (나비, 루이).

Trap 1: 제 강아지 — for beloved pets say 우리 강아지; 제 sounds distancing. Trap 2: 애완동물 thinking it's the warm word — it's correct but dated/stiff; prefer 반려동물 or just 우리 애기/강아지. Trap 3: 수컷/암컷 for a pet's sex — use 남자아이/여자아이 in casual conversation.

mistakes: Saying 제 강아지 for a beloved pet.
Koreans say 우리 강아지 ('our dog'), treating the pet as family. 제 (my) can sound distancing; default to 우리.
Calling your pet 수컷/암컷 in casual talk.
수컷/암컷 (male/female) are clinical/livestock terms. Owners say 남자아이/여자아이 for a pet's sex in friendly conversation.
Using 애완동물 thinking it's the warm word.
애완동물 is correct but stiff/dated. The modern, kinder term is 반려동물; affectionately, just 우리 애기/강아지.

english: It sheds so much (the fur falls out a lot)
usage: Polite-neutral; 털 빠지다 = fur falls out/sheds
examples: A: 요즘 집에 털이 너무 많아요. / B: 털갈이 철이라서요. 매일 빗질해 줘야 해요.
A: There's so much fur around the house lately. / B: It's because it's shedding season. You have to brush it daily.
A/B exchange showing the cause-and-solution pattern; 철 = season
털갈이 철엔 매일 빗질해 주는 게 좋아요.
In shedding season, brush it daily.
철 = season; 빗질하다 = brush the coat; frequent brushing reduces loose fur in the home
내일 강아지 미용 맡겼어요.
I dropped my dog off for grooming tomorrow.
미용 맡기다 = entrust the pet for grooming; 미용 = professional hair grooming/styling
nuance: 털 = 'fur / body hair (of an animal)', and 빠지다 = 'to fall out / come off' (intransitive). In Korean, shedding is described intransitively: 털이 빠져요 ('fur falls out'), with 털 as the SUBJECT — NOT 'the dog sheds fur' transitively as in English. So 강아지가 털을 빠져요 is wrong because 빠지다 cannot take an object; the natural forms are 강아지 털이 빠져요 or 강아지가 털이 많이 빠져요 (double-subject structure). The nearest near-synonym phrase is 털이 심하게 빠져요 ('the fur falls out severely'), intensifying the same structure. 털갈이 = the seasonal coat change/molt (털 + 갈이, 'hair-changing'), and 털갈이 철 ('shedding season') is when it's worst, usually spring and fall. Grooming vocabulary: 빗질(하다) = brushing, 미용 = professional grooming/haircut (you 맡기다 'entrust' your pet to an 애견미용실 'dog grooming salon'), 목욕(시키다) = bathing (causative — you bathe the pet). The English-speaker trap is 머리카락 ('human head hair') for animal fur — animals have 털, only humans have 머리카락. Also don't say 떨어지다 ('to drop/fall from a surface') for shedding — 빠지다 is the correct verb for hair/fur coming out.

structuredNuance.t: 털이 너무 많이 빠져요 literally means 'the fur falls out too much' — 털 = animal fur/hair (not 머리카락 which is human hair), 빠지다 = to fall out (intransitive). The sentence structure puts 털 as the subject — the fur itself 'falls out'; you don't 'shed' fur transitively.
Polite-neutral 존댓말, common small-talk among owners and with groomers or vet staff. It's a universal pet owner complaint and instantly relatable. In 반말 with a friend: 털 너무 많이 빠져.

털 빠지다 vs. 털 떨어지다: 빠지다 = come out/fall out (hair, teeth, screws — things that pull free); 떨어지다 = drop/fall from a surface (leaves, apples). For hair/fur shedding, always 빠지다. 빗질하다 (brush, owner action) vs. 미용 맡기다 (professional grooming, you take it in).
털이 심하게 빠져요 ('sheds severely'), 온 집에 털 투성이예요 ('the whole house is covered in fur'), 털 빠짐이 심한 품종이에요 ('it's a breed that sheds heavily').

Trap 1: 강아지가 털을 빠져요 (transitive) — 빠지다 is intransitive; the fur is subject. Say 강아지 털이 빠져요. Trap 2: 머리카락 for animal fur — animals have 털; humans have 머리카락. Trap 3: 털이 떨어져요 for shedding — 빠지다 is for hair/fur coming out, not 떨어지다.

mistakes: Saying 강아지가 털을 빠져요 (transitive).
빠지다 is intransitive — the fur is the subject. Say 강아지 털이 빠져요 or 강아지가 털이 빠져요.
Using 머리카락 for animal fur.
머리카락 is human head hair. Animal fur/hair is 털: 털이 많이 빠져요.
Saying 털이 떨어져요 for shedding.
떨어지다 = drop/fall (off a surface). Hair/fur coming out is 빠지다: 털이 빠져요.

english: I have to register my pet (microchip/registration)
usage: I have to register my pet
Polite; 동물등록 = the legal pet registration
Did you get the microchip done?
I put on the ID tag
인식표 = external ID tag (the other option)
examples: A: 강아지 키운 지 얼마 됐어요? / B: 한 달 됐어요. 이제 동물등록 해야 돼요.
A: How long have you had your dog? / B: One month. I have to register it now.
A/B exchange showing 동물등록 as a new-owner obligation that naturally comes up
동물병원에서 내장칩으로 동물등록 했어요.
I registered with a microchip at the vet.
내장칩으로 = 'by/with the microchip' (method marker 으로); the vet implants it
등록 안 하면 과태료 나올 수 있어요.
You can get a fine if you don't register.
과태료 = an administrative fine (not criminal); 나오다 = to be issued/come out
nuance: 동물등록 = 'animal registration' (動物登錄), the legally required registration of your dog with the local government — a real obligation that many newcomers overlook, with a 과태료 ('administrative fine') for non-compliance. You register via two methods: 내장칩 ('internal microchip', implanted at the vet) or an 외장형 인식표 ('external ID tag worn on the collar'); the microchip is the most common. After registration you receive a 동물등록증 ('registration certificate'). The verb is 등록(을) 하다 ('to register'); 동물등록 했어요 = 'I registered (the pet)'. The nearest near-synonym is 동물등록 마쳤어요 ('I completed the registration'), slightly more formal. The English-speaker trap is 가입하다 ('to sign up / join' for memberships or services) — 가입 is for subscribing to something, whereas official government record-registration is 등록; say 동물등록 했어요, never 동물 가입했어요. Note 과태료 (administrative penalty) differs from 벌금 (criminal/court fine) — pet registration non-compliance incurs 과태료. Currently dogs are legally required to register; cat registration is voluntary in most areas.

structuredNuance.t: 동물등록 (動物登錄) = 'animal registration' — the government-mandated registration of your dog. 해야 돼요 = 'I have to do it', expressing legal obligation. Registering links the pet's microchip/tag to your identity in the national database.

Polite-neutral 존댓말, exactly what you'd say to a vet, another owner, or at the 동사무소 (district office, one registration venue). In 반말 with a friend: 동물등록 해야 돼. It's a practical obligation topic, not sensitive.

내장칩 (internal microchip, permanent) vs. 인식표 (external ID tag on collar, can be lost). 과태료 (administrative fine for civil violations) vs. 벌금 (criminal/court fine) — pet registration non-compliance is 과태료. 등록하다 (register with a government body) vs. 가입하다 (join/subscribe to a service).
동물등록 is 動物登錄: 동물 (動物) = animal, 등록 (登錄) = registration/recording. The -하다 verb 등록하다 is the standard registration verb across many domains (학교 등록, 회원 등록, etc.).

Trap 1: 가입하다 for pet registration — 가입 is joining/subscribing to services; official government registration is 등록하다. Trap 2: thinking registration is optional for dogs — it is legally required in Korea. Trap 3: 벌금 for the fine — it's 과태료 (administrative), not a criminal 벌금.

mistakes: Saying 동물 가입했어요 for registering a pet.
가입하다 is for joining/subscribing (memberships, insurance). Official registration is 등록하다: 동물등록 했어요.
Thinking registration is optional for dogs.
Dog 동물등록 is legally required in Korea, with a 과태료 (fine) for non-compliance. Do it at the 동물병원 (microchip) or a 동사무소.
Saying 벌금 for the non-registration penalty.
벌금 is a criminal/court fine. An administrative penalty like this is 과태료: 과태료 나올 수 있어요.

english: How much was the vet bill?
usage: How much was the vet bill?
How much is the exam fee?
펫보험 = pet insurance; 들다 = to take out (insurance)
나오다 used for a bill 'coming out' to an amount
examples: A: 동물병원 갔다 왔어요? / B: 네, 진료비 얼마 나왔어요? / A: 검사까지 해서 십오만 원 나왔어요.
A: Did you go to the vet? / B: Yes — how much was the bill? / A: With the tests, it came to 150,000 won.
A/B exchange showing 나오다 as the natural verb for a calculated bill amount
검사까지 해서 십만 원 나왔어요.
With the tests, it came to 100,000 won.
검사 = (medical) test; -까지 해서 = 'including ...'; 십만 원 = 100,000 won (count in 만-units)
동물병원은 보험이 안 돼서 좀 비싸요.
Vets are pricey since insurance doesn't apply.
보험이 안 되다 = insurance doesn't cover it — national health insurance is humans-only
nuance: 진료비 = 'consultation / treatment fee' (診療費), the vet bill; the suffix -비 (費) is the Sino-Korean morpheme for 'fee/cost' seen in 교통비 (transport cost), 식비 (food cost), 병원비 (hospital bill). The natural, idiomatic verb for a bill is 나오다 ('to come out / be issued') — 얼마 나왔어요? = 'how much did it come out to?', the phrasing Koreans instinctively use for any calculated total. The nearest near-synonym question is 얼마였어요? ('how much was it?'), which is understandable but less specific for a tabulated bill — 나오다 is the verb that belongs here. Korean vet care is NOT covered by national health insurance (reserved for humans), so bills can surprise people; 펫보험 ('pet insurance') exists but you must 들다 / 가입하다 ('take it out / sign up') well in advance. The English-speaker trap is 가격 ('price tag of a product') for a service fee — for service bills/fees, use 비(용) or 진료비. Don't confuse 진료비 (exam/treatment fee) with 약값 ('medicine cost') — they may appear as separate line items. Currency: Korean amounts use Sino-Korean numbers + 원, counted in 만 (ten-thousands): 십만 원 = 100,000 won.

structuredNuance.t: 진료비 (診療費) = consultation/treatment fee — the vet bill. 얼마 나왔어요? = 'how much did it come out to?' using 나오다 ('come out/be issued'), the standard verb for calculated bills. The phrase is asking about the final total after seeing the vet.
Polite-neutral 존댓말, perfect at the checkout desk, with another owner, or discussing vet costs. In 반말: 진료비 얼마 나왔어? It's a common, empathetic topic among pet owners as vet costs are high in Korea.

진료비 (exam/treatment fee) vs. 약값 (medicine cost) — may be separate items on the bill. 나오다 for a calculated bill total vs. 얼마예요? which asks the listed price upfront. 가격 is for the price tag on goods, not service fees. 건강보험 covers humans; for pets you need private 펫보험.
진료비 is 診療費: 진료 (診療) = examination and treatment, 비 (費) = cost/fee. The -비 morpheme appears in 교통비, 식비, 생활비, 병원비 — all meaning 'cost of X'.

Trap 1: 가격 얼마예요? for a vet bill — 가격 is the price of a product; service fees are 비(용) or 진료비. Trap 2: 얼마였어요? for a bill total — natural but less idiomatic; prefer 얼마 나왔어요? Trap 3: assuming national health insurance covers the vet — it covers humans only; vet care requires private 펫보험.

mistakes: Asking 가격 얼마예요? for a vet bill.
가격 is the price of goods. A service fee/bill is 진료비 or 비용: 진료비 얼마 나왔어요?
Saying 얼마였어요? for the total bill.
Understandable, but for a calculated bill Koreans say 얼마 나왔어요? ('how much did it come out to'). Use 나오다 for bills.
Assuming national insurance covers the vet.
건강보험 covers humans only; vet care isn't covered, so it's pricey. For coverage you need private 펫보험, taken out in advance.

usage: Can I bring my dog in?
애견 동반 = accompanied by a dog
examples: A: 저기요, 여기 반려동물 출입 돼요? / B: 네, 이동장에 넣으시면 돼요.
A: Excuse me, are pets allowed here? / B: Yes, if it's in a carrier it's fine.
A/B exchange showing the common condition (케이지/이동장); 이동장 = pet carrier
반려동물 동반 가능한 카페 찾고 있어요.
I'm looking for a pet-friendly café.
동반 가능 = accompaniment possible (pet-friendly); common on app searches and signs
여기는 케이지에 넣으면 출입 돼요.
Here it's allowed if it's in a carrier.
케이지/이동장 = carrier; 넣다 = put (the pet) in; conditional permission is common indoors
nuance: 반려동물 = 'companion animal' (반려 '伴侶' companion + 동물 animal), the modern respectful umbrella term for pets, now standard on signs, in apps, and in media — much warmer than the older 애완동물 ('plaything animal'). 출입 = 'entry / coming and going' (出入), so 출입 돼요? = 'is entry allowed?'; 동반 = 'accompanying', so 반려동물 동반 가능 = 'pets may accompany you' = pet-friendly, the exact wording on café and store signage. To say you bring your pet in, use 데리고 들어가다 ('go in WITH a living being') — the verb 데리다 marks the companion as living; 가지고 들어가다 ('bring an object in') for a dog sounds dehumanizing and odd. The nearest near-synonym question is 강아지 데리고 들어가도 돼요? ('may I go in with my dog?'), which is slightly more conversational; 출입 돼요? is more sign/formal in register. The English-speaker trap is 허락돼요? ('is it permitted?' from 허락 'personal permission/consent') — 허락 is for person-to-person permission, not public access rules; use 출입 돼요? or 들어가도 돼요?. 동반 sounds formal/sign-like; in speech, 강아지 데리고 가도 돼요? is the casual spoken version.

structuredNuance.t: 반려동물 출입 돼요? literally means 'is pet entry/access permitted?' — 출입 (出入) = in-and-out access, 돼요? = is it okay/permitted? It's a polite public-space question. The phrase reflects real-world Korean access culture where many venues are 반려동물 동반 가능 (pet-friendly) or 금지 (prohibited).

Polite-neutral 존댓말, correct for asking staff at any venue. More casual spoken version: 강아지 데리고 들어가도 돼요? 동반 is the formal/sign register; 데리고 가다 is the everyday spoken register. With a friend: 강아지 데리고 가도 돼? (반말).

반려동물 출입 돼요? (formal/sign-style) vs. 강아지 데리고 들어가도 돼요? (everyday spoken). 반려동물 (modern, respectful) vs. 애완동물 (older, slightly dated). 데리고 (with a living being) vs. 가지고 (with an object) — the choice shows whether you're treating the animal as a companion or a thing.
출입 is 出入, 'going out and coming in' — used for access/entry to places. 반려 is 伴侶, 'companion/partner'. 동반 is 同伴, 'accompanying together'.

Trap 1: 허락돼요? for public access — 허락 is personal permission between people; for institutional access use 출입 돼요? or 들어가도 돼요? Trap 2: 강아지 가지고 들어가도 돼요? — 가지고 is for objects; use 데리고 for living companions. Trap 3: 애완동물 on formal inquiries — use 반려동물.

mistakes: Asking 허락돼요? for whether pets are allowed.
허락 is personal permission/consent. For public entry, ask 출입 돼요? or 들어가도 돼요?: 반려동물 출입 돼요?
Saying 강아지 가지고 들어가도 돼요?
가지고 (가지다) is for objects. For a living animal use 데리고: 강아지 데리고 들어가도 돼요?
Using 애완동물 on/about modern pet-friendly places.
Signs and polite speech use 반려동물 (companion animal). 애완동물 sounds dated; prefer 반려동물 동반.

english: It passed away (crossed the rainbow bridge)
usage: Gentle euphemism for a pet's death
Soft way to say a pet died
What you say to a grieving owner
examples: A: 요즘 좀 힘들어 보여요. 무슨 일 있어요? / B: 우리 강아지가 지난주에 무지개다리 건넜어요.
A: You look a bit down lately. Is everything okay? / B: My dog crossed the rainbow bridge last week.
A/B exchange showing how 무지개다리 건넜어요 is delivered as difficult news, gently
많이 힘드시겠어요, 위로의 말 전해요.
You must be hurting — my condolences.

nuance: 무지개다리(를) 건너다 = 'to cross the rainbow bridge', the same tender euphemism English uses, and the most common gentle way Koreans speak of a pet's death; 하늘나라(에) 가다 ('go to heaven/sky-country') is another soft option. You generally avoid the blunt 죽었어요 ('it died') when comforting a grieving owner — factually correct but cold; the euphemisms show respect for how deeply Koreans grieve pets. The nearest near-synonym expression is 하늘나라 갔어요, but 무지개다리 건넜어요 is the most recognized pet-specific phrase online and in communities. To express condolences: 많이 힘드시겠어요 ('you must be having a hard time') or 위로의 말 전해요 ('I offer words of comfort') are warm and appropriate. The formal funeral phrase 삼가 고인의 명복을 빌어요 (traditionally for people) is increasingly used for pets too — Koreans take pet grief seriously. The English-speaker trap is 잃어버렸어요 ('I lost it') to mean the pet died — 잃어버리다 means you misplaced or lost track of it (it ran away), a very different meaning that creates confusion. Another trap: 안락사 (euthanasia) is a heavy clinical word; don't blurt it as casual sympathy. This register is gentle 존댓말. Korea now has 반려동물 장례식장 ('pet funeral homes') and cremation services.

structuredNuance.t: 무지개다리(를) 건너다 literally means 'to cross the rainbow bridge' — 무지개 = rainbow, 다리 = bridge, 건너다 = to cross. This is the standard tender euphemism for a pet's death, shared across Korean and English pet culture. It softens the directness of 죽다 ('to die').

Gentle 존댓말, used when sharing or receiving news of a pet's death. Used in online communities (카카오톡, 인스타그램) and in person. If someone shares this, respond with 위로의 말 전해요 or 많이 힘드시겠어요 — never just change the subject. Pet grief (펫로스) is taken seriously in Korea.

무지개다리 건넜어요 (pet-specific, warmest) vs. 하늘나라 갔어요 (gentle, also used for people) vs. 세상을 떠났어요 (passed away, more formal, usually for people) vs. 죽었어요 (blunt, factual — avoid with grieving owners). 잃어버렸어요 ≠ died; it means you lost track of/misplaced the pet.
무지개다리 건너간 지 1년 됐어요 ('it's been a year since it crossed'), 사진 보면 아직도 보고 싶어요 ('I still miss it when I see photos'), 무지개다리 너머에서 잘 지내고 있을 거예요 ('it's probably doing well beyond the rainbow bridge').

Trap 1: 잃어버렸어요 to mean 'it passed away' — 잃어버리다 = lost/misplaced (it ran away); for death say 무지개다리 건넜어요. Trap 2: 죽었어요 to a grieving owner — correct but cold; use the euphemism. Trap 3: 안락사 as casual sympathy — it's a heavy clinical word; offer comfort instead: 많이 힘드시겠어요.

mistakes: Saying 죽었어요 bluntly to a grieving owner.
It's correct but cold. Use the gentle 무지개다리 건넜어요 or 하늘나라 갔어요 when comforting someone.
Saying 잃어버렸어요 to mean the pet died.
잃어버리다 = lost track of / misplaced (it ran away). For death, say 무지개다리 건넜어요, not 잃어버렸어요.
Blurting 안락사 as casual sympathy.
안락사 (euthanasia) is a heavy clinical term. Don't introduce it lightly; offer comfort: 많이 힘드시겠어요.
